# How To Use This Document {#sec-how-to-use}

This document is a thesis-facing explanation of **CN-PUP**, a Nextflow pipeline
for analysing single-cell DNA sequencing data from circulating tumor cells
(CTCs). I wrote it as both a learning document and a Methods-style companion:
it should help me understand what every step does, while also being clear
enough for examiners or future users of the code.

The document has two main roles:

1. It explains the biological and computational motivation for the pipeline.
2. It documents how the pipeline works, which files it expects, and how the
   different execution modes connect to the thesis questions.

Important internal links:

- [Thesis context](#sec-thesis-context)
- [High-level workflow](#sec-workflow-overview)
- [Input data model](#sec-input-data-model)
- [How the pipeline works](#sec-how-it-works)
- [Mode-by-mode explanation](#sec-modes)
- [Background subtraction](#sec-background-subtraction)
- [Variant caller comparison](#sec-caller-comparison)
- [Variant flowcharts](#sec-variant-flowcharts)
- [Planned extensions](#sec-planned-extensions)
- [Glossary](#sec-glossary)

This is a living technical document. Some parts describe implemented pipeline
behavior, while other parts describe planned extensions that are relevant to the
thesis but not fully implemented yet. I mark these explicitly where needed.
:::

# Thesis Context {#sec-thesis-context}

## Tumor Evolution, ITH, and Therapy Resistance {#sec-ith}

Cancer remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide, with nearly 20
million new cases and 9.7 million deaths estimated in 2022 [@bray2024global].
Although therapies have improved, relapse and treatment resistance remain major
problems, especially in late-stage disease [@gillies2012evolutionary;
@lim2019tumor]. A key reason is that tumors are not homogeneous masses of
identical cells. They are evolving populations.

Tumorigenesis is driven by the accumulation of genetic and epigenetic changes
that promote proliferation, survival, immune escape, invasion, and other cancer
hallmarks [@hanahan2022hallmarks]. Genomic instability contributes to this
process by continuously generating new alterations during tumor growth
[@requesens2024genomic]. Because tumor cells proliferate under strong selective
pressure, different subclones can emerge, compete, and disseminate.

This diversity is called **intra-tumor heterogeneity** (ITH). ITH can exist at
the level of single nucleotide variants (SNVs), copy number alterations (CNAs),
structural variants, methylation, transcriptional state, and phenotype. It has
been demonstrated by multi-region sequencing studies, where different regions of
the same tumor often contain partly distinct mutation sets
[@gerlinger2012intratumor; @jamalhanjani2017tracking]. Metastases can also be
highly heterogeneous, and recent work has shown that metastatic lesions may
contain multiple subclones rather than a single uniform population
[@albakir2023tracerx; @hessey2026metastasis].

This matters clinically because therapy can select resistant subclones. A
treatment may reduce most of the tumor burden while leaving behind cells that
already carry resistance-associated features. These cells can then expand and
drive relapse [@longley2005resistance]. Modern treatment strategies, including
combination therapy and adaptive therapy, are partly motivated by this
evolutionary view [@robert2015dabrafenib; @gatenby2009adaptive;
@zhang2017adaptive].

For my thesis, this creates the central biological problem: **to understand a
patient's tumor evolution, I need methods that can measure heterogeneity rather
than only a single consensus tumor profile**.

## Circulating Tumor Cells as a Window Into ITH {#sec-ctc-context}

ITH has traditionally been studied using multi-region tissue sampling and,
more recently, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA). Multi-region sampling is powerful
because it preserves spatial information and can reveal how different tumor
regions are related [@gerlinger2012intratumor; @jamalhanjani2017tracking].
However, repeated multi-site biopsies are difficult to perform in living
patients, especially longitudinally.

ctDNA is more accessible because it can be measured from blood. It can track
tumor burden and treatment response over time [@zhang2020ctdna]. However,
ctDNA is a mixture of fragments released from many cells, and its composition
depends on tumor shedding, cell death, tumor location, and other biological
factors [@rachman2024ctdna]. It often lacks direct cellular context.

Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) occupy an interesting middle ground. They are
intact tumor-derived cells found in the bloodstream. They can potentially be
sampled longitudinally like ctDNA, while retaining cell-level genomic context.
This makes them attractive for studying ITH and tumor evolution
[@markou2023ctcs; @zhan2023ctcmetastasis; @mitra2015emt]. CTC enumeration has
prognostic value in several cancers [@bork2015ctc], and modern single-cell
sequencing technologies now make it possible to profile CTC genomes at much
higher resolution [@wang2015singlecell; @hawsawi2024singlecell].

Several studies have used CTC sequencing to compare CTCs with tumors,
metastases, or longitudinal disease states [@pawlikowska2019ctcs;
@su2019sclc; @dutta2023minimumseq; @faugeroux2020prostatectc]. These studies
motivate the use of CTCs for asking whether blood-borne tumor cells represent
the primary tumor, metastatic lesions, specific subclones, or a distinct
circulating compartment.

## Phylodynamics and CTCs {#sec-phylodynamics}

The thesis is not only about detecting mutations. It is also about using those
mutations to infer relationships between cells and tissues. Phylodynamics
combines evolutionary relationships with population structure and dynamics
[@stadler2021phylodynamics]. In infectious disease, related ideas are used to
track how viral variants spread through populations [@cardonaospina2021covid].
In cancer, the analogous idea is to reconstruct how tumor subclones are related
and how they change over space and time.

Tumor phylogenies have been built from multi-region bulk data and from
single-cell data [@cooper2015prostate; @yates2015breast;
@singhal2024prostate]. CTC-based phylogenetic studies are newer, but they are
especially relevant to this thesis because they can connect liquid biopsy with
cell-level clonal structure [@gremmelspacher2025ctcclusters;
@dutta2023minimumseq].

The long-term goal is that CN-PUP produces reliable SNV matrices that can feed
into phylogenetic tools such as CTC-SCITE and DelSieve. This is discussed in
the [planned extensions](#sec-planned-phylogeny).

## Why CTC Variant Calling Is Difficult {#sec-ctc-challenges}

CTC sequencing is technically difficult. A single diploid cell contains only two
copies of each autosomal locus, so whole genome amplification (WGA) is usually
needed before sequencing. WGA can introduce amplification bias, allelic dropout,
false-positive variants, and uneven coverage [@wang2015singlecell]. As a
result, a variant observed in one CTC can represent:

- a true somatic mutation in a tumor subclone,
- a germline variant not properly removed,
- a WGA or sequencing artifact,
- a mapping or alignment problem,
- or a caller-specific false positive.

This is why the pipeline does not simply trust one variant caller. Instead, it
supports comparison between multiple callers and emphasizes background
subtraction using matched leukocyte and bulk blood samples. The distinction
between true CTC-specific biology and single-cell technical noise is one of the
central problems of the thesis.

## Thesis Goal Connected To The Pipeline {#sec-thesis-goal}

The thesis has two connected goals:

1. To evaluate how well CTC DNA sequencing represents the clonal composition of
   matched primary and metastatic tumor tissue.
2. To develop a robust bioinformatics pipeline for analysing CTC single-cell DNA
   sequencing and producing mutation sets suitable for overlap and phylogenetic
   analysis.

The main scientific questions are:

- To what extent do CTC SNVs overlap with matched primary and metastatic tissue?
- Can CTC sequencing alone reveal intra-patient clonal heterogeneity?
- Can longitudinal CTC sequencing detect changes in clonal composition over
  time?
- How does the answer change as more CTCs are sequenced?

CN-PUP is my working solution for the computational side of these questions.
It is designed to take aligned sequencing data and/or caller VCFs, filter and
normalize the variants, subtract likely germline/background variants, compare
callers, and produce mutation matrices for downstream analysis.

# Pipeline Purpose {#sec-pipeline-purpose}

CN-PUP stands for the internal project name **CeciNestPasUnePipeline**, but in
this document I use **CN-PUP** as the short name for the analysis workflow. The
academic description is:

> A Nextflow pipeline for SNV-based comparison of circulating tumor cells,
> matched blood-derived background samples, primary tumors, and metastases.

The pipeline currently focuses on SNVs. This is intentional. SNVs are discrete
events that can be represented in tables, compared across cells and tissues,
and converted into mutation matrices for phylogenetic inference. CNAs are
planned as a complementary layer, discussed in [CNA integration](#sec-planned-cna).

The pipeline is designed around seven practical tasks:

1. Validate patient-level and cell-level input configuration.
2. Run MonoVar jointly across single-cell BAMs when needed.
3. Split joint MonoVar output into one VCF per cell.
4. Import existing VCFs from MonoVar, HaplotypeCaller, DeepVariant, or SCcaller.
5. Filter, normalize, and subtract germline/background variants.
6. Produce comparable VCFs, mutation tables, matrices, and overlap reports.
7. Produce per-CTC variant flowcharts that summarize filtering, background
   subtraction, and sharing across CTCs or matched tissue.

# High-Level Workflow {#sec-workflow-overview}

At a high level, CN-PUP turns heterogeneous inputs into comparable per-cell,
per-caller SNV sets.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Patient TSV] --> B[CHECK_INPUTS]
    B --> C{Selected execution mode}

    C --> D[RUN_MONOVAR]
    D --> E[SPLIT_MONOVAR]

    C --> F[External VCF manifest]
    F --> G[MonoVar split VCFs]
    F --> H[HaplotypeCaller VCFs]
    F --> I[DeepVariant VCFs]
    F --> J[SCcaller VCFs]

    K[Leukocyte VCF] --> M[Background exclusion set]
    L[Bulk blood VCF] --> M

    E --> N[Filter and normalize SNVs]
    G --> N
    H --> N
    I --> N
    J --> N

    M --> O[Subtract germline/background variants]
    N --> O

    O --> P[Comparable VCFs]
    P --> Q[Long mutation table]
    Q --> R[Mutation matrices]
    Q --> S[Overlap QC reports]
    P --> U[Per-CTC variant flowcharts]
    R --> T[Phylogenetic downstream analysis]
```

The key design principle is that every caller branch eventually produces the
same contract:

```text
results/<patient_id>/comparable_calls/<caller>/<cell_id>.<caller>.comparable.vcf.gz
```

Once variants are in this comparable format, downstream scripts can merge them,
build mutation matrices, and summarize overlap. This is described in
[caller comparison and matrices](#sec-caller-comparison).

# Input Data Model {#sec-input-data-model}

CN-PUP is config-driven. Instead of hard-coding samples into the workflow, the
user describes patients, cells, BAMs, and VCFs in TSV/YAML files under
`configs/`.

## Patient Sheet {#sec-patient-sheet}

The patient sheet is the main entry point. It has one row per patient or
patient-level analysis unit.

```text
patient_id
ref_fasta
monovar_bam_list
cell_metadata
germline_mode
germline_vcf
bulk_bam
leukocyte_bam
leukocyte_vcf
```

Conceptually:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `patient_id` | Name used for output directories and grouping. |
| `ref_fasta` | Human reference FASTA used for calling and normalization. |
| `monovar_bam_list` | Text file containing BAM paths for MonoVar joint calling. |
| `cell_metadata` | Per-cell metadata table. |
| `germline_mode` | Strategy for background/germline subtraction. |
| `germline_vcf` | Precomputed germline or bulk blood VCF, depending on mode. |
| `bulk_bam` | Matched bulk BAM, currently mainly used by SCcaller. |
| `leukocyte_bam` | Matched leukocyte BAM, used for some MonoVar modes. |
| `leukocyte_vcf` | Precomputed leukocyte VCF used for background subtraction. |

Example for leukocyte-only subtraction:

```text
patient_id                 germline_mode   germline_vcf   leukocyte_vcf
patient_03_wxs_ctc_only    leukocyte_vcf   NA             /path/to/leukocyte.monovar.split.vcf
```

Example for combined leukocyte and bulk blood subtraction:

```text
patient_id                 germline_mode   germline_vcf                leukocyte_vcf
patient_03_wxs_ctc_only    combined        /path/to/bulk_blood.vcf.gz  /path/to/leukocyte.vcf
```

See [combined subtraction mode](#sec-mode-combined) for the logic.

## Cell Metadata {#sec-cell-metadata}

The cell metadata file has one row per cell:

```text
patient_id    cell_id    bam_path    cell_type
```

The `cell_id` is the biological label used downstream, such as `CTC1`,
`CTC2`, or `leukocyte`. The `cell_type` field is useful for distinguishing
CTCs from leukocytes or other sample types.

This file is important for two reasons:

1. MonoVar splitting uses it to map joint VCF samples back to cell names.
2. SCcaller and BAM QC modes use it to find per-cell BAMs.

## MonoVar BAM List {#sec-monovar-bam-list}

MonoVar expects a text file containing one BAM path per line. CN-PUP stores
this path in the patient sheet under `monovar_bam_list`.

For CTC-only MonoVar calling, the BAM list should contain only the CTC BAMs.
The leukocyte can then be used later as an external subtraction source. This
separation is useful because it avoids mixing the leukocyte into the CTC joint
calling cohort.

## External Caller Manifest {#sec-caller-vcfs}

Existing VCFs from different callers are described in `caller_vcfs.tsv`.

```text
patient_id    cell_id    caller    vcf_path    sccaller_mode
```

Supported caller names are:

- `monovar`
- `haplotypecaller`
- `deepvariant`
- `sccaller`

The manifest lets CN-PUP compare callers without rerunning all caller software
inside the same workflow. This is especially useful while testing multiple
variant callers on public and Tzu-generated datasets.

Example:

```text
patient_03_wxs_ctc_only    CTC1    monovar           /path/to/CTC1.monovar.split.vcf
patient_03_wxs_ctc_only    CTC1    haplotypecaller   /path/to/CTC1.haplotypecaller.filtered.vcf.gz
patient_03_wxs_ctc_only    CTC1    deepvariant       /path/to/CTC1.deepvariant.vcf.gz
```

## Params YAML {#sec-params-yaml}

For reproducible runs, I prefer a params YAML file over a long command line.

```yaml
patients: configs/patients.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only_compare.tsv
caller_vcfs: configs/caller_vcfs.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only_compare.tsv
outdir: results
run_monovar: false
run_external_callers: true
run_comparison: true
run_snv_report: true
min_total_depth: 20
min_alt_reads: 4
min_vaf: 0.0
genome: GRCh38
```

This keeps the analysis easier to rerun and easier to document.

# How The Pipeline Works {#sec-how-it-works}

This section explains the pipeline step by step. The mode-specific subsections
are in [Pipeline Modes](#sec-modes).

## Step 1: Read Configuration {#sec-step-read-config}

Nextflow starts from the patient sheet:

```nextflow
Channel
  .fromPath(params.patients, checkIfExists: true)
  .splitCsv(header: true, sep: '\t')
```

Each row is converted into a tuple containing the patient ID, reference FASTA,
BAM lists, metadata, germline mode, and background files. This is the main
data structure that carries patient-level information through the workflow.

## Step 2: Validate Inputs {#sec-step-validate}

The `CHECK_INPUTS` process verifies that required files exist and that the
selected `germline_mode` is valid. For example:

- `ref_fasta` must exist.
- `monovar_bam_list` must exist if `--run_monovar true`.
- `cell_metadata` must exist for MonoVar, SCcaller, or BAM QC modes.
- `germline_vcf` must exist in `precomputed_vcf` mode.
- `leukocyte_vcf` must exist in `leukocyte_vcf` mode.
- both bulk and leukocyte evidence are expected in `combined` mode.

Validation output is written to:

```text
results/validation/<patient_id>.input_check.txt
```

## Step 3: Generate Or Import Variant Calls {#sec-step-callers}

CN-PUP can either run some callers internally or import precomputed VCFs.

Currently:

- MonoVar can be run internally from BAM files.
- SCcaller can be run internally from existing BAMs.
- HaplotypeCaller and DeepVariant are imported as external VCFs.

This split is pragmatic. DeepVariant and HaplotypeCaller are often run through
separate established workflows, while CN-PUP focuses on standardizing their
outputs for comparison.

## Step 4: Filter To Comparable SNVs {#sec-step-filter}

Each caller has slightly different VCF structure and assumptions. The pipeline
therefore converts raw caller output into a comparable SNV-only representation.

For common callers (`monovar`, `haplotypecaller`, `deepvariant`), the downstream
filter requires:

- `FILTER` is `PASS` or `.`,
- genotype is non-reference,
- depth is at least `min_total_depth`,
- alternate read count is at least `min_alt_reads`,
- variant type is SNV.

The current defaults are:

```yaml
min_total_depth: 20
min_alt_reads: 4
min_vaf: 0.0
```

These values should be treated as working thresholds, not universal truth. They
may need adjustment by dataset, sequencing depth, WGA method, and caller.

## Step 5: Normalize Variants {#sec-step-normalize}

Before variants can be compared, they are normalized with `bcftools norm`.
Normalization ensures that equivalent variants are represented consistently
relative to the same reference FASTA.

The workflow uses:

```bash
bcftools norm -f "$REF_FASTA" -m -any
```

This matters because comparisons such as `bcftools isec` depend on matching
chromosome, position, reference allele, and alternate allele.

## Step 6: Prepare Background Exclusion Set {#sec-step-exclusion}

Matched leukocyte and bulk blood samples are used to remove variants that are
likely germline or recurrent technical/background calls.

The exclusion set can come from:

- a precomputed bulk/germline VCF,
- a leukocyte VCF,
- a leukocyte split from MonoVar joint calling,
- or a combined leukocyte plus bulk blood set.

The combined strategy is currently important for the thesis because I want to
subtract both:

1. the single-cell leukocyte signal, which may capture WGA/cell-level artifacts,
2. the bulk blood signal, which provides a stronger germline/background profile.

See [Background Subtraction](#sec-background-subtraction) for details.

## Step 7: Subtract Background Variants {#sec-step-subtract}

The normalized cell/caller VCF is compared against the normalized exclusion VCF
using `bcftools isec`.

```bash
bcftools isec -C -w1 cell.norm.vcf.gz exclusion.norm.vcf.gz
```

Conceptually, this keeps variants present in the cell/caller VCF but absent
from the background VCF. The result is a comparable VCF enriched for candidate
somatic CTC variants.

## Step 8: Build Tables And Matrices {#sec-step-matrices}

Comparable VCFs are converted into long mutation tables and binary matrices.
The comparison branch reuses scripts under:

```text
bin/mutation_matrix/
```

The main products are:

- long mutation table,
- caller-specific and merged mutation matrices,
- CTC-SCITE input matrices,
- overlap QC reports.

# Pipeline Modes {#sec-modes}

CN-PUP can be run in different modes depending on which part of the analysis I
want to perform.

## Validation-Only Mode {#sec-mode-validation}

Validation-only mode is the default. It checks whether the patient sheet is
readable and whether the selected inputs are available.

Example:

```bash
nextflow run main.nf \
  --patients configs/patients.tsv
```

Use this mode when:

- setting up a new patient,
- checking server paths,
- testing a new config,
- or debugging missing files.

Output:

```text
results/validation/<patient_id>.input_check.txt
```

## MonoVar Calling Mode {#sec-mode-monovar}

MonoVar is designed for single-cell variant calling and can jointly call
variants across multiple single-cell BAMs. In CN-PUP, MonoVar is run from a
patient-level BAM list.

Example:

```bash
nextflow run main.nf \
  -profile conda \
  --patients configs/patients.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only.tsv \
  --run_monovar true \
  --monovar_script /path/to/monovar.py \
  --monovar_threads 6
```

Internally, CN-PUP runs `samtools mpileup` and pipes the result into MonoVar.
The main output is:

```text
results/<patient_id>/raw_calls/monovar/<patient_id>.monovar.vcf
```

MonoVar calling is useful because it explicitly models single-cell data and
jointly considers multiple cells. However, I still compare it with
HaplotypeCaller and DeepVariant because caller choice can strongly influence
the apparent mutation landscape.

## MonoVar Splitting Mode {#sec-mode-monovar-split}

MonoVar produces a joint VCF containing multiple samples. For downstream
comparison, CN-PUP splits this into one VCF per cell.

Outputs:

```text
results/<patient_id>/split_calls/monovar/<cell_id>.monovar.split.vcf
results/<patient_id>/split_calls/monovar/<patient_id>.monovar.split_sample_map.tsv
```

The sample map is important because it records how VCF sample columns were
matched to biological cell IDs.

## External Caller Comparison Mode {#sec-mode-external}

External comparison mode imports already-generated VCFs from `caller_vcfs.tsv`.
This is the main mode for comparing MonoVar, HaplotypeCaller, and DeepVariant
on the same CTCs.

Example:

```bash
nextflow run main.nf \
  -profile conda \
  --patients configs/patients.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only_compare.tsv \
  --run_external_callers true \
  --run_comparison true \
  --caller_vcfs configs/caller_vcfs.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only_compare.tsv
```

Or with the params file:

```bash
nextflow run main.nf \
  -profile conda \
  -params-file configs/params.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only_compare.yml
```

The external branch standardizes each VCF and produces comparable files:

```text
results/<patient_id>/comparable_calls/<caller>/<cell_id>.<caller>.comparable.vcf.gz
```

## Leukocyte Subtraction Mode {#sec-mode-leukocyte}

In leukocyte subtraction mode, the patient sheet uses:

```text
germline_mode = leukocyte_vcf
```

and `leukocyte_vcf` points to a VCF generated from the matched leukocyte.

This mode is useful when:

- a leukocyte VCF is already available,
- no bulk blood VCF is ready yet,
- or I want to specifically estimate how many CTC calls are also seen in a
  single-cell leukocyte.

Conceptually, this subtracts variants detected in the leukocyte from each CTC
VCF. Such variants may include germline variants, WGA artifacts, recurrent
alignment errors, or other background calls.

## Bulk Blood Subtraction Mode {#sec-mode-bulk}

Bulk blood subtraction uses a bulk/germline VCF as the exclusion set.

In the patient sheet:

```text
germline_mode = precomputed_vcf
germline_vcf  = /path/to/bulk_blood.vcf.gz
```

This mode is useful because bulk blood generally provides a stronger and more
complete germline profile than a single leukocyte. A bulk sample has many cells
and is less affected by single-cell WGA noise.

For the thesis, this is important because it helps distinguish somatic CTC
variants from inherited variants.

## Combined Leukocyte Plus Bulk Blood Mode {#sec-mode-combined}

Combined mode is the preferred mode once both background sources are available.

In the patient sheet:

```text
germline_mode = combined
germline_vcf  = /path/to/bulk_blood.vcf.gz
leukocyte_vcf = /path/to/leukocyte.vcf
```

CN-PUP normalizes both VCFs, merges them into one exclusion set, and subtracts
that combined set from each CTC/caller VCF.

Biologically and technically, the two background sources are complementary:

- **Bulk blood** is better for germline subtraction because it has broad,
  high-confidence coverage across many blood cells.
- **Single-cell leukocyte** is useful because it went through a more similar
  single-cell workflow and may reveal WGA-like or single-cell-specific artifacts.

For my thesis, this mode best matches the goal of retaining candidate somatic
CTC variants while removing both germline and background technical signal.

## SCcaller Mode {#sec-mode-sccaller}

SCcaller can be run internally from existing cell BAMs and a matched bulk BAM.
The current implementation assumes BAM files already exist; it does not perform
full FASTQ preprocessing.

Required inputs:

- `cell_metadata`,
- `bulk_bam`,
- `ref_fasta`,
- `--sccaller_script`,
- `--sccaller_hsnp_vcf`.

Example:

```bash
nextflow run main.nf \
  -profile conda \
  --patients configs/patients.sccaller.tsv \
  --run_sccaller true \
  --run_comparison true \
  --sccaller_script /path/to/sccaller_v2.0.0.py \
  --sccaller_hsnp_vcf /path/to/bulk.hg38.hsnp.biallelic.dbsnp.vcf
```

SCcaller-specific modes include:

| Mode | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `so_true` | Require SCcaller internal `SO=True`. |
| `external_bulk` | Ignore `SO`, then subtract external bulk/background VCF. |
| `so_true_and_external_bulk` | Require `SO=True` and subtract external background. |
| `no_bulk` | Diagnostic mode without bulk subtraction. |

## VEP Filtering Mode {#sec-mode-vep}

The VEP stage is intended to annotate comparable VCFs and filter using
population allele frequency and COSMIC-related information.

The motivation is that a variant found at high population frequency is less
likely to be a private somatic tumor mutation. However, known cancer-associated
variants may need to be retained even if they require special interpretation.

This mode is still an optional downstream stage. It should be used carefully
because annotation databases, cache versions, and genome builds must match the
analysis.

## SNV Report Mode {#sec-mode-report}

The SNV report mode is intended to summarize results in a human-readable form.
For thesis work, this will be useful for turning raw comparison outputs into
figures and tables that can be interpreted without manually opening every VCF.

## BAM QC Mode {#sec-mode-bam-qc}

BAM QC mode is optional and uses alignment-level metrics to evaluate sample
quality. This matters for single-cell sequencing because low coverage, uneven
coverage, high duplication, or poor mapping can make a cell unreliable for
variant interpretation.

The long-term goal is to connect QC metrics with downstream variant counts and
caller behavior. For example, a CTC with unusually many private SNVs but poor
coverage uniformity may be more suspicious than a CTC with similar SNV counts
and high-quality alignment metrics.

# Variant Calling Strategy {#sec-variant-calling}

## Why Compare Multiple Callers? {#sec-why-multiple-callers}

Single-cell variant calling is difficult enough that I do not want to rely on
one caller without comparison. HaplotypeCaller, DeepVariant, MonoVar, and
SCcaller make different assumptions and may behave differently on WGA-amplified
single-cell DNA.

The comparison is useful for three reasons:

1. **Robustness:** variants found by multiple callers may be more credible.
2. **Sensitivity:** some callers may recover variants missed by others.
3. **False positive estimation:** callers that produce many CTC-private calls
   also found in leukocyte/background may be less reliable for this data type.

This comparison is not only technical. It directly affects the biological
interpretation of ITH. If one caller produces many private variants, this could
look like high heterogeneity, but it may actually reflect artifacts.

## HaplotypeCaller {#sec-haplotypecaller}

HaplotypeCaller is widely used for germline variant calling and can be applied
to single-cell BAMs as a baseline caller. It was not originally designed for
WGA-amplified single-cell cancer genomes, so its output must be interpreted
carefully. In CN-PUP, HaplotypeCaller VCFs are imported as external VCFs and
standardized.

## DeepVariant {#sec-deepvariant}

DeepVariant uses a machine-learning-based approach to variant calling. Like
HaplotypeCaller, it is often robust in standard sequencing contexts, but its
behavior on single-cell WGA data must be evaluated empirically. In CN-PUP,
DeepVariant VCFs are imported and processed through the same comparable-call
branch as other external callers.

## MonoVar {#sec-monovar-caller}

MonoVar is specifically relevant because it was designed for single-cell DNA
variant calling. It jointly models multiple cells, which can help distinguish
true variants from single-cell noise. CN-PUP can run MonoVar internally and
then split its joint output by cell.

## SCcaller {#sec-sccaller-caller}

SCcaller is another single-cell-oriented caller. It can use information from a
matched bulk sample and heterozygous SNPs. In CN-PUP, SCcaller can be run from
existing BAMs, then standardized into comparable VCFs.

# Filtering, Normalization, and Background Subtraction {#sec-background-subtraction}

## Why Background Subtraction Is Central {#sec-why-subtraction}

The thesis question is about somatic tumor heterogeneity, not germline
variation. Therefore, germline and background variants must be removed before
interpreting CTC-specific or tissue-shared variants.

Subtraction also helps with single-cell artifacts. If a variant is detected in
a CTC and also in a leukocyte processed in a similar way, it may be a recurrent
artifact or background call rather than a true tumor mutation.

## Leukocyte Versus Bulk Blood {#sec-leuko-vs-bulk}

Leukocyte and bulk blood evidence answer slightly different questions.

| Background source | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Single-cell leukocyte | Similar single-cell processing and WGA context. | One cell only; sparse and noisy. |
| Bulk blood | Better germline representation and more stable coverage. | Less similar to single-cell WGA artifacts. |

For this reason, the most useful subtraction mode for the thesis is likely
`combined`, where both are used.

## What Subtraction Does Not Prove {#sec-subtraction-limits}

After subtraction, a variant is not automatically a true somatic CTC mutation.
It is only absent from the chosen background set. Remaining variants can still
include artifacts, especially if:

- coverage is low,
- alternate read support is weak,
- the locus is difficult to map,
- WGA introduced errors,
- or the background sample lacks coverage at that locus.

Therefore, subtraction is a filtering step, not a final biological proof.

# Caller Comparison And Mutation Matrices {#sec-caller-comparison}

## Comparable VCFs {#sec-comparable-vcfs}

The comparable VCF is the main standardized output. It contains filtered,
normalized variants after optional background subtraction.

Example path:

```text
results/patient_03_wxs_ctc_only/comparable_calls/deepvariant/CTC1.deepvariant.comparable.vcf.gz
```

The value of this format is that downstream code can treat all callers in a
similar way.

## Long Mutation Tables {#sec-long-tables}

Comparable VCFs are converted into long tables where each row represents a
variant observation in a sample/caller combination. This is easier to merge,
filter, summarize, and inspect than raw VCFs.

A long table can answer questions such as:

- Which variants are seen in CTC1?
- Which variants are shared between CTC1 and CTC2?
- Which variants are called by both MonoVar and DeepVariant?
- Which variants overlap with metastasis tissue?

## Mutation Matrices {#sec-mutation-matrices}

Mutation matrices represent variants as rows and samples as columns. A value of
`1` means the variant is present in that sample; `0` means absent or not called.

This format is useful for:

- CTC overlap analysis,
- subclone detection,
- phylogenetic reconstruction,
- comparing the number of sequenced CTCs with recovered mutation diversity.

## Overlap QC {#sec-overlap-qc}

Overlap QC reports summarize how much call sets overlap across cells and
callers. This is important for judging whether a caller produces many private
variants or whether there are shared patterns consistent with clonal structure.

For the thesis, overlap can be examined at several levels:

- CTC versus CTC,
- CTC versus primary tumor,
- CTC versus metastasis,
- CTC versus leukocyte,
- CTC versus bulk blood,
- caller versus caller.

# Variant Flowcharts {#sec-variant-flowcharts}

The pipeline includes a first implementation of a **per-CTC variant flowchart**
report. This report is inspired by flow diagrams used in CTC sequencing papers,
where the variant set is progressively divided into biologically meaningful
groups.

For each sample/caller pair, CN-PUP writes:

```text
results/<patient_id>/reports/variant_flowcharts/variant_flow_summary.tsv
results/<patient_id>/reports/variant_flowcharts/variant_flowcharts.md
results/<patient_id>/reports/variant_flowcharts/mermaid/<cell>.<caller>.variant_flow.mmd
```

The TSV is the machine-readable version. The Mermaid files are the visual
version and can be rendered directly in Quarto.

Metastasis or primary tissue overlap can be enabled with an optional tissue VCF
manifest:

```bash
nextflow run main.nf \
  -profile conda \
  -params-file configs/params.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only_compare.yml \
  --tissue_vcfs configs/tissue_vcfs.tsv
```

The manifest format is:

```text
patient_id    sample_id      sample_type    caller       vcf_path
patient_03    metastasis_1   metastasis     deepvariant  /path/to/metastasis.vcf.gz
patient_03    primary_1      primary        deepvariant  /path/to/primary.vcf.gz
```

The current flowchart tracks:

| Count | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `raw_input_snvs` | SNVs present in the original input VCF for that sample/caller. |
| `normalized_snvs` | SNVs remaining after caller-specific QC filtering and normalization. |
| `seen_in_bulk_blood` | Normalized SNVs also seen in the bulk blood exclusion VCF, if available. |
| `seen_in_leukocyte` | Normalized SNVs also seen in the leukocyte exclusion VCF, if available. |
| `removed_by_any_background` | SNVs removed by the final background subtraction step. |
| `comparable_snvs` | Final SNVs retained for downstream comparison. |
| `shared_with_metastasis` | Retained SNVs also seen in metastasis VCFs, when those are configured. |
| `shared_with_at_least_one_other_ctc` | Retained SNVs also found in at least one other CTC for the same caller. |
| `shared_with_all_ctcs` | Retained SNVs found in all CTCs for the same caller. |
| `non_synonymous` | Retained SNVs annotated as non-synonymous, when annotation is present. |
| `listed_db_or_cosmic` | Retained SNVs with dbSNP/COSMIC-like annotation, when annotation is present. |
| `predictive_protein_impact` | Retained SNVs with high/moderate or damaging-like protein impact annotation, when annotation is present. |

The report is designed to answer questions such as:

- How many variants did the caller produce initially?
- How many were removed by QC filters?
- How many overlap with bulk blood or leukocyte background?
- How many candidate somatic variants remain?
- Are retained variants shared with other CTCs?
- Are retained variants shared with metastasis tissue?

Example Mermaid structure:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A["Raw input SNVs<br/>1200"] --> B["After QC filters and normalization<br/>640"]
  B --> C["Seen in bulk blood exclusion<br/>180"]
  B --> D["Seen in leukocyte exclusion<br/>95"]
  B --> E["After background subtraction<br/>410"]
  E --> F["Shared with metastasis<br/>52"]
  E --> G["Shared with at least one other CTC<br/>130"]
  E --> H["Shared with all CTCs for this caller<br/>12"]
  E --> I["Non-synonymous<br/>80"]
  I --> J["Listed in dbSNP/COSMIC annotation<br/>26"]
  J --> K["Predicted protein impact<br/>14"]
```

::: {.callout-warning}
The tissue VCF manifest is currently used only by the flowchart report. A later
pipeline extension should promote primary and metastasis VCFs to first-class
comparison samples so they also appear in the main mutation matrices.
:::

# Current Patient 03 WXS Comparison Setup {#sec-patient03-setup}

The current working comparison config is:

```text
configs/patients.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only_compare.tsv
configs/caller_vcfs.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only_compare.tsv
configs/params.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only_compare.yml
```

The caller manifest contains:

- 21 MonoVar split VCFs,
- 21 HaplotypeCaller filtered VCFs,
- 21 DeepVariant VCFs.

At the moment, the config is set to leukocyte-only subtraction:

```text
germline_mode = leukocyte_vcf
```

Once the bulk blood VCF is available, the patient sheet should be updated to:

```text
germline_mode = combined
germline_vcf  = /path/to/bulk_blood.vcf.gz
leukocyte_vcf = /path/to/leukocyte.vcf
```

Then the same params-file command can be rerun:

```bash
nextflow run main.nf \
  -profile conda \
  -params-file configs/params.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only_compare.yml
```

# Output Interpretation {#sec-output-interpretation}

## Main Output Directories {#sec-output-dirs}

Typical output structure:

```text
results/
  <patient_id>/
    raw_calls/
    split_calls/
    processed_calls/
    normalized_calls/
    comparable_calls/
    caller_comparison/
    germline_exclusion/
    logs/
  validation/
```

Important directories:

| Directory | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `raw_calls/` | Raw caller output generated by CN-PUP. |
| `split_calls/` | Per-cell MonoVar VCFs after splitting. |
| `processed_calls/` | Filtered caller VCFs before final normalization/subtraction. |
| `normalized_calls/` | Normalized VCFs. |
| `comparable_calls/` | Final per-cell, per-caller VCFs after standardization. |
| `caller_comparison/` | Merged tables, matrices, and overlap reports. |
| `logs/` | Process logs for debugging and reproducibility. |

## How I Should Read The Results {#sec-reading-results}

A practical interpretation workflow is:

1. Check `results/validation/` to confirm the intended files were used.
2. Check logs for failures or suspicious filtering behavior.
3. Count variants before and after subtraction.
4. Compare variant counts across callers and cells.
5. Inspect overlap reports.
6. Use mutation matrices for clonal and phylogenetic analysis.

If a CTC has many more private variants than all others, I should not
immediately interpret it as a highly divergent subclone. I should first check
coverage, depth, WGA quality, caller agreement, and leukocyte/bulk overlap.

# Planned Extensions {#sec-planned-extensions}

## FASTA And Reference Preparation {#sec-planned-fasta}

A future module should validate and prepare reference FASTA files. This could
include:

- checking that `.fai` exists,
- checking that sequence dictionaries exist when required,
- validating chromosome naming consistency,
- indexing missing reference files,
- recording reference genome version in pipeline metadata.

This matters because mismatched references can silently break variant
normalization and comparison.

## Bulk Blood Variant Calling {#sec-planned-bulk-calling}

The current workflow can subtract a bulk blood VCF, but it does not yet run
DeepVariant or HaplotypeCaller on the bulk blood BAM internally. A future mode
could add:

```text
bulk_bam -> HaplotypeCaller/DeepVariant -> bulk_blood.vcf.gz -> exclusion set
```

This would make the combined subtraction mode more automated.

## Primary And Metastasis Comparison {#sec-planned-metastasis}

For the thesis, CTCs need to be compared with matched primary and metastatic
tissue where available. This requires adding tissue-level VCFs to the
comparison model.

Possible design:

```text
sample_id    sample_type    caller    vcf_path
CTC1         ctc            deepvariant    ...
primary      primary        deepvariant    ...
metastasis1  metastasis     deepvariant    ...
bulk_blood   blood          deepvariant    ...
```

This would allow mutation classes such as:

- shared by CTC and primary,
- shared by CTC and metastasis,
- shared by all tumor compartments,
- CTC-only,
- tissue-only.

## CNA Integration {#sec-planned-cna}

Copy number alteration analysis is planned as a second layer after SNV analysis.
CNA profiles could help:

- confirm clonal relationships inferred from SNVs,
- identify large-scale genomic events shared between CTCs and tissues,
- interpret SNV calls in deleted or amplified regions,
- detect subclonal structure that is not visible from SNVs alone.

For example, if a region is deleted in several cells, SNV absence in that region
may not mean the mutation was never present. Conversely, variants called in
regions with inconsistent copy number may need special caution.

## Phylogenetic Downstream Analysis {#sec-planned-phylogeny}

The final thesis analysis will likely use mutation matrices as input for
phylogenetic tools such as CTC-SCITE and DelSieve. CN-PUP should therefore
produce matrices with clear assumptions:

- which caller was used,
- which background subtraction was used,
- which depth thresholds were used,
- whether missing calls are treated as absence or unknown,
- which cells were excluded due to QC.

This is important because phylogenetic inference is sensitive to false
positives, false negatives, allelic dropout, and missing data.

## Sampling Saturation Analysis {#sec-planned-saturation}

One thesis question is how the number of sequenced CTCs affects the recovered
mutation profile. A future analysis module could repeatedly sample subsets of
CTCs and measure:

- number of unique variants recovered,
- overlap with primary tumor,
- overlap with metastasis,
- number of inferred subclones,
- stability of phylogenetic tree structure.

This would help answer whether mutation information plateaus after a certain
number of CTCs.

# Reproducibility {#sec-reproducibility}

CN-PUP uses Nextflow because it makes the workflow more reproducible and
modular. Each process has declared inputs and outputs, and Conda environments
can be used to manage software dependencies.

Main reproducibility principles:

- keep sample definitions in config files,
- keep commands in params files or documented scripts,
- record reference genome paths and versions,
- record caller versions,
- keep raw caller outputs separate from filtered/comparable outputs,
- use Git to track changes in workflow code and config templates.

Example reproducible run:

```bash
nextflow run main.nf \
  -profile conda \
  -params-file configs/params.patient_03_wxs_ctc_only_compare.yml \
  -resume
```

# Limitations And Cautions {#sec-limitations}

CN-PUP is under active development. Important limitations include:

- HaplotypeCaller and DeepVariant are currently imported as external VCFs, not
  run internally.
- Bulk blood VCF generation is not yet automated.
- CNA analysis is not yet implemented.
- Phylogenetic analysis is downstream/planned rather than fully integrated.
- Thresholds such as `min_total_depth` and `min_alt_reads` are working defaults.
- Single-cell false positives and allelic dropout remain major interpretation
  problems even after filtering.

The most important conceptual caution is that a final comparable VCF is not a
perfect truth set. It is a filtered hypothesis set. Biological conclusions
should be based on overlap patterns, caller agreement, background subtraction,
QC metrics, and consistency with matched tissue data.

```bash

```

# Glossary {#sec-glossary}

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| CTC | Circulating tumor cell. |
| ITH | Intra-tumor heterogeneity. |
| SNV | Single nucleotide variant. |
| CNA | Copy number alteration. |
| WGA | Whole genome amplification. |
| VCF | Variant call format. |
| BAM | Binary alignment map file. |
| Germline subtraction | Removing variants likely inherited or present in matched normal tissue. |
| Background subtraction | Broader term including germline and technical/background calls. |
| Comparable VCF | CN-PUP standardized, filtered, normalized VCF used for downstream comparison. |
| Mutation matrix | Table encoding variant presence/absence across cells or samples. |
